beats.headline: Why is your business logic buried in 50 lines of infrastructure?
beats.subline: Stop polluting your services with logging, metrics, and transaction code.
beats.narration: If your transferMoney method is 80 percent boilerplate, you have a cross-cutting concern problem. AOP extracts this noise into reusable aspects, keeping your domain logic clean and focused.

beats.title: Aspects vs Services
beats.narration: Aspects sit outside your services. Through a process called weaving, Spring wraps your beans in a proxy that intercepts calls, running your cross-cutting logic before or after the target method.

beats.title: Defining Pointcuts

steps.explanation: Targets methods marked with your custom tag.

beats.narration: Pointcuts are predicates. They define exactly where your advice runs. You can match by package, bean type, or custom annotations, combining them with boolean logic to target specific operations.

beats.title: Spring AOP vs AspectJ
beats.narration: Spring AOP is sufficient for 99 percent of enterprise apps. Use full AspectJ only if you need to advise private methods, field access, or objects created with the new keyword.

beats.title: Part 1 Locked In
beats.nextPartTeaser: Up Next: The hidden proxy trap that breaks your transactions →
beats.narration: That is the AOP foundation. In Part 2, we expose the self-invocation trap that silently bypasses your proxies.

beats.headline: Why does your @Transactional annotation suddenly stop working?
beats.subline: It is not a bug—it is a fundamental limitation of the proxy pattern.
beats.narration: If you call a method on this inside the same class, you bypass the proxy entirely. Your transaction and logging annotations will simply never fire.

beats.title: The Self-Invocation Trap

steps.explanation: Ignored because the proxy was never entered.

beats.narration: When you call this.save, you are hitting the raw object. The proxy is never triggered, so the transaction manager never starts. The database update happens without any transactional safety.

beats.title: Proxy Bypass Sequence
beats.narration: The call enters the proxy, then the target. Once inside, the target calls itself via this. The proxy is completely skipped. The advice chain is never executed.

beats.title: The Fix: Self-Injection

steps.explanation: Forces the call through the proxy.

beats.narration: The cleanest fix is injecting an ObjectProvider for the service itself. Calling the proxy bean ensures the interceptor chain executes, keeping your transactions and logging intact.

beats.title: Part 2 Locked In
beats.nextPartTeaser: Up Next: Building a custom @Loggable annotation →
beats.narration: Avoid the self-invocation trap by always calling through the proxy. In Part 3, we build a custom @Loggable annotation to measure method latency.

beats.headline: How do you log execution time without touching business code?
beats.subline: Custom annotations combined with @Around advice are your secret weapon.
beats.narration: Stop writing System.currentTimeMillis in every service. Let's create a declarative @Loggable annotation that automatically profiles your methods and warns on slow performance.

beats.title: The Annotation
beats.narration: Retention Policy Runtime is mandatory. Without it, the JVM discards the annotation before Spring can see it. Now, we define our threshold to flag slow methods.

beats.title: The Advice
beats.narration: The @Around advice gives you full control. You capture the start time, call proceed to run the target, and then calculate the elapsed duration. It is clean, reusable, and testable.

beats.title: Advice Types
beats.narration: Choose your advice wisely. Use @Before for simple validation, but reach for @Around when you need to manipulate the return value or measure latency across the entire call.

beats.title: Part 3 Locked In
beats.nextPartTeaser: Up Next: Mastering aspect order and precedence →
beats.narration: You have a custom aspect. In Part 4, we tackle aspect ordering—ensuring your security checks run before your transactions.

beats.headline: What happens when your transaction starts before your security check?
beats.subline: You waste database connections and leak data. Ordering is not optional.
beats.narration: If your transaction opens before your security check, you risk leaking database connections on unauthorized requests. Precedence is the final piece of the AOP puzzle.

beats.title: The Onion Layers
beats.narration: Spring aspects behave like an onion. Lower order numbers run first on the way in, and last on the way out. Always put security at the very outer layer.

beats.title: Enforcing Order
beats.narration: Use the @Order annotation to explicitly define precedence. By setting security to 1, you guarantee it executes before any other aspect, protecting your downstream resources effectively.

beats.title: Verification
beats.caption: Check your bean order in logs
beats.narration: Enable debug logging for the AOP package to see the chain order. It confirms exactly how your aspects wrap the target, preventing hidden performance or security bugs.
